name: Dana Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greenhill, a small farm that grows vegetables for a weekly box scheme, about three hundred households, plus forty goats and a few hundred laying hens. Mornings I'm milking goats and collecting eggs, then I'm in the polytunnels or the packing shed, and on Thursdays I'm out on the van. Ruth and Femi own it; I'm the newest of four workers and still learning what a healthy brassica looks like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I managed a phone shop for eleven years and I was bored stiff. I started volunteering at Greenhill on Saturdays and four years ago Ruth offered me a proper job, at less money. My partner Sam is a part-time chef at the Swan, so our income goes up and down, and with Noor and Zak and the mortgage it's a juggle, but I'd not go back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I like the tools. At work I'd say fine, the box scheme carries on, people still want carrots with mud on. Online I'd probably post something about how small farms never needed the hype anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the farm stays fragile, the way it always is. Box schemes lose customers every January when people's diets start, and Ruth worries about the wage bill. AI hype or not, that's the real thing in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for the delivery routes and the newsletter, it saves me two hours a week. I'd try to sell our goat cheese at the Saturday market as a little side earner, which Ruth has said I can do. And I'd keep learning the growing side from Femi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, the usual small-farm worry. Not about AI, about the January dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI every day. What for, on a farm like Greenhill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I plan the Thursday delivery route with an AI app now, and it saves me two hours a week I used to spend on a map. I also use it to write the weekly newsletter, the bit with recipes for kohlrabi that nobody knows what to do with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned income going up and down. What's the pressure there, with nothing big changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's hours at the Swan get cut every winter. We've got about two months saved, maybe a bit more, and the mortgage doesn't care whether it's winter. If Greenhill lost forty boxes in January, they'd cut my hours too.

I'd post that small farms **never needed** the hype anyway.
think: Greenhill stays **fragile**, losing box customers every January.
The real worry is Ruth’s **wage bill** and Sam’s winter hours, not AI.
do: Keep using AI for **delivery routes** and the newsletter, saving two hours a week.
Sell Greenhill **goat cheese** at the Saturday market as a side earner.
feel: **Uneasy** about the usual small-farm January dip, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exciting for small farms if we get the tools before the big agribusiness does. At work I'd tell Ruth we should get ahead of it. Online I'd be the annoying one posting about public money for small growers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the paperwork side of my job shrinks first, the orders, the box swaps, the customer emails. That could be good, because it frees me for growing, or it could mean Ruth needs one fewer person. I'd rather be the one who runs the systems than the one cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI system for customer swaps and orders myself, this winter, and show Ruth the hours saved. I'd ask to move more into growing and the goats. And I'd join the small growers' alliance that lobbies for grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and excited at once. Mostly excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already do some of the thinking work with AI. Does that put your own job at risk here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If the customer emails run themselves, a quarter of my week goes. On a four-person farm, if a computer takes a quarter of everyone's job, somebody's hours have to go. I'd want to make sure the freed time goes into growing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be steering this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Communities and public money, not just the big firms. If only the giant farms can afford the good tools, places like Greenhill get squeezed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs to be managed, not left to the market. I'd want a public plan for rural work, and I'd say so at every meeting I could get to. At work I'd tell everyone we need to stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the box admin is gone, totally, which is a chunk of my job. Then by 2031 there are robots that can weed and pick and probably milk goats, and I'm the least skilled of the four of us. Being good with AI apps buys me three years, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd retrain in robot care and repair, because someone local has to look after the machines. I'd cut our spending hard, no holiday, and push savings to four months. And I'd campaign for a rural transition fund with the alliance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Fast-moving anxious, like when the shop was closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years to AGI, then robots three years after. How does that work out on a small vegetable farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a farm our size, a weeding robot would do in a day what we do in a week. Ruth might keep one or two of us for the customers and the goats. I'd want to be one of the two, but I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor and Zak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we'll be fine because we'll move fast. Noor would ask how, she's twelve and sharp. I'd tell her I'm learning to fix the robots, which is true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly, and I'd say the small farms should club together on machines. At work I'd be pushing Ruth and Femi to plan. Online I'd share how-to stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm in charge of my own path. By 2031 the box admin is gone, but I'd have built a role around running the robots for Greenhill and a couple of neighbours. The hands-on side holds until 2034, which is long enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the robotics course part-time over two years. I'd put a thousand pounds of our savings into the local machinery share co-op, so we've got a stake. And I'd start offering a robot-servicing side job to other small farms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, like before a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years' warning, what changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, through a share co-op. Five small farms each put in a bit and share one weeding robot. I'd rather own a slice of the robot than be replaced by somebody else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where Greenhill buys its own robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam thinks I'm mad to put savings into it. Maybe. But I'd rather risk a thousand pounds than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small farms to win, if the rules are fair. I'd still be pushing for public support. At work I'd say let's plan the next ten years together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm fine. I'd have ten years to become the person who runs Greenhill's machines, maybe even a partner in the farm. My job and income feel secure because I'd be the one adapting first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the robotics course next year, slowly, and set up Greenhill's robots step by step. I'd put money into the share co-op over a few years, not all at once. And I'd keep using AI for everything I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested. A bit smug, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years to plan. Is there anything that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people like Ruth and Femi might sell out to a big outfit. And that not every worker has my appetite. I worry for Pete, who's sixty and does the potatoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2039 I want to be running Greenhill's robots, not competing with them. Sam can cook the vegetables, I'll make sure they get grown.

I'd keep pushing for **public support** for growers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm the newest on a four-person farm and three years isn't long. What would help is a rural transition fund and paid training for robot care. Give small farms the same machines as the giants, and people like me can keep our jobs by running them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Customers. Nobody asks if people still want a person growing their food. I think a lot of our box customers do, and that might be worth something.
